intro.technical: ANTAR chains six engines. TOPOHYDRO turns coarse climate into a per-node daily water balance; XYLEM converts that water stress into a mechanistic probability that trees suffer hydraulic failure; MNEME is the statistical counterpart fitted to satellite-observed dieback; MERISTEM asks where each species' climate niche and thermal treeline lie; REFUGIUM combines hazard into multi-scenario viability and robust-refugium scores; AEGIS chooses what to plant where under a budget, hedging against the worst plausible futures. This page describes what is implemented, which in several deliberate and logged ways differs from the original concept note.
intro.plain: Think of six helpers passing a baton. The first works out how wet or dry each hillside really is. The second asks how much dryness a tree can take before it fails. The third looks at satellite pictures for trees that actually died. The fourth asks where each species is comfortable and how high up trees can grow. The fifth asks which places stay safe across many possible futures. The sixth uses all of that to suggest where a limited budget does the most good.

engines.name: TOPOHYDRO — climate and water balance
engines.status: Fitted on real data. Two inputs are still flagged placeholders: budburst GDD (200) and the calm-clear-night fraction (0.3).
technical: Temperature is moved from the reference pixel's elevation to the node's own elevation, $T(x,d)=T_{\text{ref}}(d)+\Gamma_{m}\,[z(x)-z_{\text{ref}}]+\delta_{\text{CAP}}(x,d)$. $\Gamma_m$ is a monthly lapse rate fitted to Armenian GHCN-D stations (roughly $-7.6$ K/km in summer and $-4.9$ K/km in winter); $\delta_{\text{CAP}}\le0$ is a cold-air-pooling term on $T_{\min}$ driven by terrain concavity.

Precipitation uses a monthly log-linear elevation gradient, so it cannot go negative; elevation explains at most about 1% of its variance, so the correction is small. The reference year is 2019 from CHELSA-daily (about 1 km). Wind, shortwave, longwave and dew point are ERA5-Land annual cell means, each given the seasonal cycle of the observation-based ISIMIP3a GSWP3-W5E5 product (2015–2019, 0.5°), $x(d)=\bar x_{\text{cell}}\,s_x(d)\,\rho_x(d)$, where $s_x$ has mean 1 and $\rho_x$ is the model's monthly future/baseline ratio in a scenario. Until 2026-10-06 these four were repeated unchanged on every day of the year, which removed most of the summer water deficit; that has been replaced. Pressure is still the annual mean.

Potential evapotranspiration is carried as three formulations (FAO-56 Penman–Monteith, the default shown; Priestley–Taylor; energy-only). Actual evapotranspiration comes from a single-bucket soil model with capacity $W_{\max}=(\theta_{\text{fc}}-\theta_{\text{lim}})\,z_{\text{root}}$, with soil parameters from SoilGrids via the Saxton–Rawls pedotransfer functions and matric potential $\psi_s=\psi_{\text{sat}}(\theta/\theta_{\text{sat}})^{-b}$ (Clapp–Hornberger).

Indices: $\mathrm{CWD}=\sum_d(\mathrm{PET}_d-\mathrm{AET}_d)$; $\mathrm{WSI}=\sum_d\max\{0,(\mathrm{REW}_{\text{crit}}-\mathrm{REW}_d)/\mathrm{REW}_{\text{crit}}\}$; $\mathrm{GDD}=\sum_d\max(T_d-5,0)$; growing season = days with daily mean $\ge0.9\,^\circ$C; GST = mean temperature over those days.

Rooting depth is species-specific (2.9 m deciduous forest, 3.9 m conifer forest, 9.5 m arid juniper; Canadell et al. 1996), so each functional group experiences its own water-stress signal rather than one shared value.
plain: Imagine each patch of ground as a bucket of soil water. Rain fills it; sun and wind empty it. How deep a tree's roots reach decides how big its bucket is — a deep-rooted juniper has a far bigger bucket than a shallow-rooted beech.

The 'climatic water deficit' is simply how much extra water the tree would have drunk if the bucket hadn't run dry. Mountains are cooler — every 100 metres uphill is roughly half a degree to three-quarters of a degree colder — so we take a coarse weather record and slide it up or down the slope to fit each spot.

engines.name: XYLEM — mechanistic hydraulic-failure hazard
engines.status: P50 and slope are real values from congeneric XFT records. Other traits (stomatal-closure potential, phase-transition temperature, lethal PLC, capacitance) are order-of-magnitude placeholders. Juniper is skipped: only one XFT record exists, so no variance can be estimated.
technical: A two-phase time-to-failure model. Phase 1: the soil dries until its water potential reaches the group's stomatal-closure potential. Phase 2: with stomata shut, the tree drains its own water store through the cuticle. The buffer $B=C\,(\psi_{\text{close}}-\psi_{\text{crit}})$ is consumed at $E_{\min}=g_{\min}(T)\,\mathrm{VPD}_{24}/P_{\text{atm}}$, and the hydraulic-failure index $\mathrm{HFI}=\sum_{\text{closed days}}86400\,E_{\min}/B$ reaches 1 at $\psi_{\text{crit}}$ (P88 for angiosperms, P50 for conifers). $\mathrm{HFI}\ge1$ is the model's definition of hydraulic failure.

Uncertainty is carried explicitly with a two-level Monte Carlo: 50 outer draws of group-level $P_{50}$ and slope (spread from the between-record variation in XFT) $\times$ 200 inner draws of individual trees. $h^{\text{mech}}$ is the share of individuals that fail per outer draw; the map shows its mean and the spread across outer draws is the trait-knowledge uncertainty.

No individual-level variance exists in the pulled data, so individual spread is set to 0.5$\times$ the group-level spread, a documented placeholder rather than a measurement. Only $P_{50}$ and slope are sampled; closure potential, capacitance, $g_{25}$, $T_p$ and the lethal loss of conductivity are held at placeholder values.
plain: A tree is a straw drawing water from the soil up to its leaves. In a drought the water in the straw is pulled so hard that air bubbles form and the straw stops working. Each species' straw fails at a different level of suction.

First the tree shuts its leaf pores to save water. After that it can only leak a little through its leaf skin, slowly draining a reserve tank. The model asks whether the dry spell lasts longer than the tank. Because we don't know every tree's exact straw, we simulate thousands of slightly different trees and count how many fail.

engines.name: MNEME — statistical hazard from observed dieback
engines.status: Built and run on a rebuilt panel of every qualifying forest pixel (57,504 pixels, 570,175 pixel-years), not fitted: the strict rule finds 162 dieback onsets, enough for the fit, but the same rule finds 92 pixels with a persistent decline against 1,370 with a persistent rise, so the events cannot be told from changes in the satellite record itself, and no hazard is claimed. A continuous vitality-response analysis stands in for the missing events: no detectable drought response overall, and XYLEM's drought-stress ranking is supported for oak only.
technical: The panel follows forest pixels only: 30 m pixels whose nine 10 m sub-points all lie on a closed-forest class of the national Ecosystem Map, every such pixel of each 30-arcsecond climate cell (57,504 in 219 cells), so that every pixel of a cell shares the cell's climate and has its own vitality series, canopy height (Sentinel-2 vegetation height model, 2019) and elevation.

Dieback labels come from a standardised annual kNDVI anomaly, $z_t=(k_t-\tilde k)/s$ with the median $\tilde k$ and standard deviation $s$ of the preceding ten years of the same pixel. An onset fires at $t$ when $z_t<-2$ and $z_{t-1}\ge-2$ (the decline starts there), no harvest or fire is flagged (Hansen Global Forest Change loss, MODIS burned area) in year $t$ or $t-1$, and $z$ does not rise above $-1$ in the two following seasons. Each pixel counts once and then leaves the risk set.

The person-year panel carries climate covariates ($\mathrm{CWD}$, $\mathrm{VPD}_{24}$, GDD, mean temperature) split into within-cell deviations and between-cell means (a Mundlak decomposition), plus canopy height. The intended fit is a complementary log-log hazard model, $\operatorname{cloglog}(h)=\ln\Delta+\eta$, stacking a GLM and a monotone gradient-boosted model under spatial block cross-validation. It is fitted only with at least 10 events per column of the design (90 here) and only if the rule finds at least twice as many declines as rises on the mirrored series (below). The panel has 162 events, but 92 declines against 1,370 rises, so it is not fitted.

Two checks say what the events mean. The rule is also run on the mirrored series, which counts persistent rises: there are far more rises (1,370 pixels) than declines (92), because the Jul–Aug composites rest on a median of one to eight valid observations before 2014 and thirteen to thirty-one after, and the mean anomaly steps up in 2013. With the year effect shared by all pixels removed the rule finds many more onsets (1,171) but still fewer pixels with a decline (518) than with a rise (989). A shuffled-year placebo was rejected as a null: series are autocorrelated and carry level shifts, so shuffling invents collapses.

Vitality response (needs no events). With pixel fixed effects, $z_{pt}=a_p+\beta\,x_{n(p)t}+e_{pt}$, where $x_{nt}$ is the within-cell departure of the climatic water deficit in standard deviations (1 SD is about 65 mm) and the pixel-years with a harvest or fire in the previous ten years are left out. Errors are clustered by cell and by year and the larger standard error is used. The model is judged by leave-one-year-out $R^2$, by year fixed effects, by restricting to composites with at least five valid observations and to 2014–2019, and on the series with the common year effect removed.

Check of XYLEM's ranking. For each species group, $z_{pt}$ is regressed on $x_{nt}$ and $x_{nt}$ times the within-group rank of XYLEM's mechanistic hazard in the pixel's cell. The expectation fixed in advance is a negative interaction; it is read from the 95% interval alone (supports, contradicts or inconclusive).

Not applied: stand age, the drought-legacy cross-basis and stand-interaction terms (no real stand-age or tree-ring data for Armenian plots), and misclassification correction (no labelled sample). The components are built and unit-tested.
plain: Satellites photograph the forest every year. A stand whose greenness drops far below its own recent normal, stays low for several seasons, and wasn't logged or burned is a likely dieback. We now look only at pixels that are really forest, and we check that the harvest and fire records actually work (the first version of that record was wrong).

Across more than fifty thousand forest pixels the rule finds 162 events in ten years: enough to try a model. But the satellite record itself changes over time (more and better pictures after 2014), which makes greenness jump up for everybody at once, so a rule built to find collapses finds far more 'sudden recoveries' (1,370 pixels) than collapses (92). Events that cannot be told from that are not used to fit a model.

So we ask a gentler question that needs no events: in a drier-than-usual year, is a forest pixel less green than usual? Overall the answer is 'not detectably'. Where the physical model says trees should be most at risk, oak stands do show a steeper dip in dry years, which is modest support for the model's ranking; beech does not tell us either way.

engines.name: MERISTEM — climate niche and treeline
engines.status: Adult-niche models refitted for 6 of 7 species with the real water-balance climatic water deficit of each species' group (Pinus kochiana skipped: 8 records). Cross-validated skill is modest: mean Boyce index 0.27 to 0.44 for beech, hornbeam and the two oaks, and near zero for the junipers, whose real water deficit is zero everywhere at their assumed 9.5 m rooting depth, so that predictor carries no information. Three models (Fagus orientalis, Carpinus betulus, Quercus macranthera; mean Boyce index at least 0.3, a gate fixed before the refit) decide where a species group may be planted. The attainable-height and growth model is not fitted.
technical: A penalised logistic presence–background model is fitted per species (pooling disparate species gave an unstable result and was rejected). Presences are GBIF records; background is target-group. Predictors: winter minimum temperature, GDD5 and mean vapour-pressure deficit (CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ normals), the real water-balance climatic water deficit of the species' group for 2019 (TOPOHYDRO, with the group's rooting depth; it replaces the earlier PET − precipitation proxy), and clay, sand, silt and organic carbon (0–30 cm). Records without a usable soil or ERA5-Land value are dropped (3,157 of 3,524 points kept).

Skill is the Boyce index under spatial block cross-validation (0.25° blocks). The per-species values are on the Models page; several folds are negative, so the niche scores are a rough guide. Refitting with the real water deficit raised the mean Boyce index of Carpinus from 0.25 to 0.37, of Quercus macranthera from 0.14 to 0.38 and of Quercus iberica from −0.07 to 0.27, and lowered the junipers' from 0.34 to about 0.09–0.10 (their real deficit is zero, so the proxy carried more information).

Use in decisions. A site is within a species' niche when its fitted score reaches the score below which 10% of the species' own records fall. A species model is used only if its mean Boyce index is at least 0.3 (a gate fixed before the refit); a group is niche-supported where any of its passing species is, and a group with no passing species is reported as not assessed rather than treated as suitable everywhere. For a scenario member the winter minimum and growing degree days come from CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ for the member's period and climate model, the water deficit is the member's own, and the vapour-pressure deficit, which has no future layer, is scaled with the warming at constant relative humidity (a lower bound on its rise).

Potential treeline elevation inverts the lapse relation for the elevation at which growing-season mean temperature equals the thermal threshold, $z_{\text{tl}}=z+(T_{\text{tl}}-\mathrm{GST})/\Gamma$, with $T_{\text{tl}}=6.45\,^\circ$C (the global Körner–Paulsen value) and $\Gamma=-6.89$ K/km the April–September fitted lapse rate.
plain: The niche model asks: where do these trees already grow, and what do those places have in common? Then it scores every other place by how much it resembles a place where the tree grows. The scores are a rough guide, not a precise map.
Treeline is simpler. Trees stop where summers are too cold to grow wood. Because it gets colder as you go up, there is a height above which it is always too cold. Warming moves that height upward.

The niche model now uses the real dryness of each place instead of a rough stand-in, and it improved for beech, hornbeam and the oaks. The decision layer only plants a species group where its model says the species can grow in today's climate, and only the models that work reasonably well are allowed to decide; the others are shown but not used.

engines.name: Treeline change
engines.status: Climatic ceiling only — not a forecast of where forests will stand. Global threshold, not an Armenia calibration. One representative year per horizon.
technical: For every GCM × SSP × horizon member, the real monthly ISIMIP3b temperature change (5-year future window minus 2015–2019) is added to the daily 2019 reference series. Growing-season temperature is then recomputed from the shifted daily series with the pipeline's own functions and inverted for treeline elevation. On the 25-node grid the 2019 reconstruction matches the full pipeline's stored value exactly (max difference 0.0000 °C); on the dense grid that comparison could not be repeated, because the stored file covers other cells. The dense run needs only terrain, which is read from the cached inputs, so it also covers the 67 nodes whose soil or ERA5-Land data are incomplete (921 nodes in all).

GST is a mean over the days that clear 0.9 °C. Warming adds cold shoulder-season days to that set, which can pull the mean down even though every day warmed. A measurable share of cell–member pairs therefore show a treeline drop under warming, mostly in low-warming members (the Treeline page states the current figure). This is a property of the growing-season definition, not a prediction that treelines fall; it is reported rather than hidden.
plain: We ask how far uphill the 'too cold for trees' line moves under each climate model and emissions path. For the strongest warming it moves several hundred metres.

One quirk worth knowing: if warming merely lengthens the season, the extra early-spring and late-autumn days are cold, and they drag the season's average temperature down. In a few cool-ish cases the model's ceiling therefore appears to sink a little. That is an artefact of how 'season average' is defined, so treat small negative values as 'roughly no change'.

engines.name: REFUGIUM — viability and robust refugia
engines.status: Reduced scope: one year of hydraulic survival only (the growth/height term is not fitted, so it is fixed at 1). The robust-refugium test now has all three criteria that can be computed: ensemble viability (a), buffer index (b) and area of applicability (c). Criterion (d), stand connectivity and size, is not checked, and no pine cell can pass (c) because the mapped pine forest is too small to define an area of applicability.
technical: Viability is $V=\prod_y(1-h_y)\cdot\mathbb{P}[\text{height ok}]$. With one year and no growth model, $V^{(1)}=1-h^{\text{mech}}$ for each of the 50 outer draws.

The risk-averse score is $\operatorname{median}(V)-\lambda\,\mathrm{IQR}(V)$ across the ensemble ($\lambda=0.5$). A cell is a robust refugium when three tests hold: (a) $\mathbb{P}_\omega[V\ge v^\ast]\ge\rho$ with $v^\ast=0.6$ and $\rho=0.8$; (b) the buffer index $B_i=(\bar E_{\mathrm{reg},i}-E_i)/\mathrm{sd}(E)>0$, where $E$ is the mean of the standardised climatic water deficit, water-stress integral and growing degree days and $\bar E_{\mathrm{reg},i}$ its mean over the nodes within three grid steps (about 20 km); (c) the cell lies inside the group's area of applicability (Meyer & Pebesma 2021), built from the nodes where the group's forest covers at least 2% of the cell on the Ecosystem Map, in the space of mean temperature, precipitation, growing degree days, water deficit and water-stress integral.

Criterion (b) holds by construction at about half the nodes (those cooler or wetter than their surroundings), so it ranks places rather than certifying them; the number of cells passing all three tests changes by at most 6% when the radius is 2 or 5 steps. The water-stress integral stands in for growing-season vapour-pressure deficit, which is not stored per node. Criterion (c) flags a cell or a scenario member whose climate no mapped stand of the group experiences instead of asserting it is viable there: at 2100 under SSP5-8.5 it removes between about 30% and 85% of the nodes, depending on the climate model.

Future viability uses the same engines on the delta-method climates: 5 GCMs (GFDL-ESM4, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MRI-ESM2-0, UKESM1-0-LL) × 3 SSPs (126, 370, 585) × 3 horizons (2050, 2080, 2100). Temperature and precipitation use the ISIMIP3b monthly change applied to 2019 CHELSA-daily; shortwave, longwave, wind and vapour pressure use the ISIMIP3b monthly ratio (future 5-year mean over the model's own 2015–2019 mean) applied to their seasonal shape, so humidity, radiation and wind change with the scenario. Cloudiness changes only as far as the model's own shortwave does; pressure and CO2 are held at present values.
plain: A refugium is a spot where trees are likely to make it through even if our knowledge of the physics is a bit off. So we don't trust the average alone; we check whether a spot looks safe across many plausible versions of the model.

The future runs take a real recent year and ask 'what if every month were as much warmer or drier as each climate model projects?'. Humidity, wind and sunshine change with the scenario too, following each model's own monthly change; only air pressure and CO2 are held at today's values.

A spot counts as a refugium only if it passes three tests: the trees survive in most versions of the model; the spot is cooler or wetter than its surroundings, so it is shielded from regional stress; and its climate resembles places where this kind of forest already stands, so the model is not guessing far beyond what it has seen.

engines.name: AEGIS — robust planting portfolio
engines.status: Real inputs, with stated simplifications: only species groups with a usable niche model are ranked (broadleaf and oak; pine has none) and each is planted only where its niche model puts it today; benefit varies only by species group and cost only by method (no real data links method to survival); only the restoration methods are ranked, on each cell's open land; only planting has Armenian cost data (a range); water limits are not applied. The plan shows which cells and species groups to prioritise under a budget, not which method works best (see Known gaps).
technical: At most one option (functional group $\times$ intervention method) is chosen per unit to maximise $(1-\lambda)\,\mathbb{E}[B]+\lambda\,\mathrm{CVaR}_\alpha[B]$ ($\alpha=0.8$) subject to total cost $\le$ budget (Rockafellar–Uryasev linear programme). Benefit in scenario $c$ = viability $\times$ niche support $\times$ 417 USD/ha/yr $\times$ 75% (World Bank 2023: the national ecosystem-services value, and the share of it that a restored degraded hectare adds). Niche support is 1 when the group's niche model puts the cell within the niche under that member's climate and 0 otherwise; an option is allowed in a cell only if the group is within its niche in the 2019 climate. A group enters only if a niche model of one of its species passes the quality gate (mean Boyce index at least 0.3); pine does not, so it is not ranked.

Eligibility excludes protected areas (WDPA) and cells with more than 50% human-modified land within 500 m (settlements, cropland, buildings, quarries; Ecosystem Map of Armenia). Already-forested cells are deliberately not excluded because three of the eight methods act on existing forest.

Sweeping $\lambda$ from 0 to 1 traces the mean–CVaR frontier; the distance between its ends is the price of robustness. Options that another option beats on every cell and scenario (equal or higher benefit, equal or lower cost) are removed before solving, which does not change the optimum, and each solve is accepted when its proven bound is within 1% of the best plan found.

An optional cap requires that the options of one species group together take at most a share $s$ of the treated area, $\sum_{u,j\in g}A_{uj}x_{uj}\le s\sum_{u,j}A_{uj}x_{uj}$; a cap of one half with two groups would force their areas to be exactly equal, so 80% and 65% are offered. Dominance is then applied only between options of the same group on the same area, so the cap is never violated by the presolve. Solves are accepted within 0.01% of the best possible.
plain: It works like building an investment portfolio, but for planting sites. Given a budget, which mix of species and methods should go where so that even the unlucky futures still turn out acceptably, not just the average one?

A species is only put where its range model says it can grow today, and a place that stops suiting it in a future scenario counts for nothing in that scenario. That makes the plan genuinely hedge: some places look good on average but poorly in the worst futures, and the plan weighs those. A limit on how much of the plan one species group may take spreads the risk further, at a small cost.

placeholders.name: Budburst GDD threshold
placeholders.effect: Sets the late-frost-day count (frost days from budburst to the warmest day of the year).
placeholders.state: Placeholder. A cited species-specific threshold could not be verified: the primary source uses a non-linear growing-degree-hours model and no simple threshold exists in it. Late-frost days are the days with minimum temperature below −2 °C between budburst and the warmest day of the year (the peak of a 15-day running mean of daily mean temperature), so autumn and winter frosts are not counted. Measured on the 854 dense nodes: at 200 °C·d the mean is 0.01 days in 2019 and 9 nodes have a frost day (at most 2); at 100 °C·d 41 nodes do, at 50 °C·d 108 and at 25 °C·d 261 (mean 1.3 days); at 300 °C·d none. For GFDL-ESM4 SSP5-8.5 in 2100 it is 12 nodes at 200 °C·d and 492 at 25 °C·d. Because the count is almost zero at the placeholder, late frost is not mapped and cannot yet tell sites apart; a species-specific budburst threshold is needed first. Literature checked again on 2026-10-08: Murray, Cannell and Smith (1989, Journal of Applied Ecology) give day-degrees above 5 °C from 1 January that depend on prior chilling and rank beech (Fagus sylvatica) as the latest and most demanding of fifteen species; Malyshev et al. (2022, Frontiers in Plant Science) count degree-days above 5 °C from 1 January for beech but report no threshold; a chilling-and-forcing chamber study of beech, pedunculate oak and lime (Global Change Biology, 2026) reports forcing in growing degree hours. None gives a field degree-day threshold, and none concerns Fagus orientalis or the Caucasian oaks, so no species-specific value is substituted: that needs Armenian or Caucasian phenology records (for example from the national forest inventory plots).

placeholders.name: Calm-clear-night fraction
placeholders.state: Placeholder. ERA5-Land has no cloud-cover band (checked directly), so the planned fix does not exist. Measured: sweeping it from 0 to 0.6 changes the hydraulic hazard by at most 0.0002 (oak 0.0608 to 0.0607 in 2019; 0.1018 to 0.1017 for SSP5-8.5 in 2100) and the number of dense nodes with a late-frost day by a few (3 to 16 of 854 in 2019; 8 to 17 in 2100).

placeholders.name: Individual-tree spread
placeholders.effect: Width of the inner Monte Carlo loop.
placeholders.state: Placeholder. No individual-level variance exists in the pulled data.

placeholders.name: Stomatal-closure potential, phase-transition temperature, lethal PLC, capacitance
placeholders.state: Placeholders. No unit-compatible XFT field exists for them.

placeholders.name: Rooting depth
placeholders.state: Sourced (Canadell et al. 1996), but biome-level rather than species-level.

placeholders.name: Treeline thermal threshold
placeholders.state: Global Körner–Paulsen default, not calibrated to Armenia.

placeholders.name: Niche quality gate and presence threshold
placeholders.effect: Which species niche models decide where a group may be planted, and where a site counts as inside a niche.
placeholders.state: Choices, not calibrated. The gate was fixed before the refit; it admits Fagus orientalis, Carpinus betulus and Quercus macranthera and excludes Quercus iberica (0.27) and the junipers. A different gate or omission rate would change which cells are eligible.

placeholders.name: MNEME fit conditions
placeholders.value: 10 events per design column; declines ≥ 2 × rises
placeholders.effect: Whether a hazard model is fitted at all.
placeholders.state: Rules of thumb fixed before the large run. The second condition (the rule must find at least twice as many pixels with a persistent decline as with a persistent rise) is what stops a hazard being fitted to changes in the satellite record; it is not met (92 against 1,370).

placeholders.name: Refugium buffer radius and training share
placeholders.value: 3 grid steps (about 20 km); forest ≥ 2% of the cell
placeholders.effect: Criterion (b) and the area of applicability of criterion (c).
placeholders.state: Choices. The number of cells passing all three tests changes by at most 6% for radii of 2 and 5 steps; the 2% forest share sets which cells define where a group's forest is known to stand.

placeholders.name: Species-group cap
placeholders.effect: How far the plan is spread over species groups.
placeholders.state: Illustrative values chosen to be clear of 50%, which with two groups would force equal areas.

known_gaps: Atmospheric inputs (2026-10-06 correction): until this date wind, shortwave, longwave and humidity were ERA5-Land annual means repeated on every day and held in every scenario. A test on 23 Armenian cells showed this removed most of the summer water deficit (broadleaf: 14 mm vs 114 mm with the real seasonal cycle) and flattened the scenario response (change in deficit under SSP5-8.5 by 2100: +4 mm vs +212 mm). The earlier 'viability stays flat across scenarios' result was largely this artefact. Every result shown on this site has been recomputed with the seasonal, scenario-dependent forcing (2026-10-06 to 2026-10-07); results from the earlier forcing are withheld.

Sample size: the survival, scenario and decision results use the dense Armenia-only grid (854 nodes with a valid water balance, about 6.5 km apart; the treeline, which needs only terrain, 921 nodes). The fits that predate it (the forest-cover check) still use the 25-node grid. Every layer in the UI is labelled with the grid it comes from, and a dense result is used only once it covers the grid almost completely.

MNEME: the first panel followed one pixel per grid node whatever its land cover and read a harvest and fire layer that said 'disturbed' everywhere (a masking error), so its 'no dieback events' result was an artefact. The rebuilt panel (57,504 forest pixels in 219 cells, 2010–2019) has 162 onsets, but the vitality record is not homogeneous: 92 pixels with a persistent decline against 1,370 with a persistent rise, and a step in 2013, so the events cannot be told from changes in the record and no hazard is fitted. Climate covariates stop in 2019 (CHELSA-daily precipitation), while onsets cluster in 2021. No georeferenced dieback records, stand ages or tree-ring series were found for Armenia; the data request note lists who may hold them.

Decision layer: benefit depends on the species group (survival times niche support) but not on the method, so the restoration methods are equally effective by construction and the cheapest one always wins; the plan can say where to treat and with which species group, not which method works best. Only broadleaf and oak are ranked; pine has no usable niche model (8 records) and is not assessed. The niche comes from sparse, collection-biased occurrence records with modest skill, and survival is hydraulic only: establishment and growth are not modelled. Cells are treated whole although the species may suit only part of a cell. The three forest-management methods and mining reclamation are not ranked (no benefit figure, no site data).

Against mapped forest cover at the 23 sampled cells inside Armenia, predicted viability shows only weak positive rank correlation (broadleaf ρ = 0.28, p = 0.19; oak ρ = 0.19, p = 0.38), which is not statistically significant at n = 23. An earlier 'significant' result (n = 61) included cells over neighbouring countries and has been retracted. Pine could not be tested because no mapped pine cover falls in the sampled windows.

The spatial range of correlation could not be resolved even on the dense grid (854 nodes): the semivariogram of elevation-detrended water deficit still rises almost linearly out to about 130 km (a straight line fits better, R² 0.99, than an exponential model, 0.96, whose practical range of about 650 km lies beyond the lags used). Residual spatial dependence therefore extends across much of the country, the 25 km blocks used for the niche models do not make their folds independent, and the hazard model, when it can be fitted, should be validated by leaving whole regions out.

Blocked cross-validation for the hazard model and the hydraulic emulator are built and unit-tested but have not been applied to results: they need a fitted hazard model and a wall-to-wall run. The variance partition is applied to the scenario ensemble (climate model, emissions path, horizon; the Treeline and Models pages), but not to the trait-parameter uncertainty of the hydraulic model (Sobol' indices), and the ensemble has one run per model and path, so internal variability is not separated from the model effect.
TRY plant-trait data and CORDEX regional projections are deferred to version 2.1.

Map colouring: the surface is an inverse-distance interpolation between model nodes (854 on the dense grid), not a model run at every pixel, and the maps show no interpolation score. Colours between nodes are indicative; the node values are the results.

Map borders: marz borders come from geoBoundaries (Wikimedia-derived, 2005) and are approximate to kilometres; the national outline, forest, woodland and water come from the national Ecosystem Map. An official cadastral boundary would replace the marz lines.

Forest cover on the map is today's mapped cover (Ecosystem Map classes 31–37 forest, 39/41/43/44 woodland). It is not projected forward: the model gives where conditions stay viable, not where forest will stand.

Refugium criteria: the buffer index and the area of applicability are computed for the 2019 climate and for each of the 45 members on the dense grid, with the water-stress integral standing in for vapour-pressure deficit. Pine has too little mapped forest (3 cells) for an area of applicability, so no pine cell is a robust refugium; stand connectivity and size (criterion d) is not checked.

Niche models: the water-deficit predictor is one year (2019) beside 1981–2010 climatological normals, and the scores are relative suitabilities from sparse, collection-biased GBIF records, with fold-to-fold swings in skill. The junipers' real water deficit is zero everywhere, which removed information their earlier proxy carried, so their models are weaker; they have no hydraulic-survival result either, so they are not in the decision layer. Pinus kochiana (8 records) has no model, so pine is not assessed.
